speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering clause 8 of Bill No. C-126. Shall the clause carry?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
During the recess hour I spoke to the minister about the effect of his proposal upon the operations of western grain elevators. The hon. gentleman did reply to certain queries and suggestions put forward by the former minister of agriculture in this field, but I should like further clarification with respect to the working of extended hours at certain periods of the year.
As I explained to the minister during the supper recess, there is a period of about three weeks in the fall during which farmers go to the elevators at, possibly, seven o'clock in the morning or ten o'clock at night with samples of grain to be tested. The elevator men have no objection to this practice and we would like to see that it can be continued.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that under the terms of clauses 9 and 10 this necessary longer period of hours is possible.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Thank you.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 9-Excess hours under ministerial permit.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Certain aspects of this clause are important as far as the general application of the bill is concerned and what I have to say about clause 9 should, I feel, be considered in relation to the provisions of clause 10 which makes it clear that in emergency situations hours of work over and above the normal hours can be permitted.

Canada Labour Code
Clause 9 as I understand it allows an extension of normal working hours in certain circumstances on application to the minister. It is therefore an important clause, as far as it will concern the administration of this bill when it becomes law. The aspect of the matter which most concerns me at the moment is that the minister is permitted to take certain action under this clause on the application of an employer or of an employers' organization. It is true that the clause provides that if an application is received from an employer the minister must take into consideration the conditions of employment and the welfare of the employees. However, having regard to the emergency provisions set out in clause 10 the issuance of such a permit should not be the result of a unilateral decision by an employer or an employers' organization.
I know that in British Columbia the circumstances in which a board concerned with industrial relations is allowed to grant overtime permits on the unilateral application of an employer has in the past created considerable difficulties and resulted in a good deal of argument between employers and employees. As I understand it, the present bill is designed to operate within the collective bargaining framework upon which all of us are increasingly agreed. In the circumstances envisaged by clause 9 I believe any application to the minister should be the result of a prior understanding reached between an employer and his employees. Let me point out that we are not now dealing with emergency situations-breakdowns and that sort of thing. We are talking about situations in which for a period of time and for certain reasons the normal provisions restricting overtime are to be waived. Therefore, without further lengthy argument I should like to propose an amendment to clause 9 as it now stands, and move:
That subclause (1) of clause 9 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
9. (1) On the joint application of an employer or an employer's organization, and the employees or employees organization, the Minister, having regard to the conditions of employment in any industrial establishment and the welfare of the employees, may, by a permit in writing, authorize hours to be worked by any class of employees therein in excess of the maximum hours of work prescribed by or under section 6.
It is apparent at once that the only change I am proposing to the clause as presently drafted is the inclusion of the words "and the employees or employees' organization". In other words, the purpose of my amend-
ment is to ensure that there be a prior understanding between an employer and his employees involved before any application is made to the minister for permission to work in excess of the hours set forth in the bill as being a normal working day or working week.
I hope that the committee will see fit to accept what I consider to be a very reasonable proposal without any lengthy argument or discussion upon the subject matter of my amendment.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in connection with this amendment there is one question I would like to raise immediately. It concerns the problem that would arise in a plant or an operation where no employees' organization existed and where this particular necessity would arise. In some cases, especially in the north, where we are accustomed to issuing, under the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, overtime permits in somewhat the same way, the casual nature of work at times may make it quite impossible to consult an employees' organization. In the absence of an employees' organization, how is the application to be made on behalf of the employees?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the terms of my amendment, where I say "employees or employees' organization", is designed to deal with just that kind of situation, in other words, that in the absence of an official collective bargaining agent, duly certified, there would have to be submitted, I suppose in this case by the employer, evidence in writing that the employees, by their signature or other appropriate means, had indicated that they were agreeable to the application being presented by the employer.
I deliberately tried to phrase my amendment to take care of the situation that the minister has mentioned, where in the absence of an official collective bargaining agent it would be possible for the minister to set up the appropriate machinery for the employees to indicate their position in regard to an application. It seems to me that this is simply a matter of the appropriate administrative machinery being established. It would mean, in my view, that the minister, prior to dealing with an employer's application in the case where there was a group of employees who were not formerly recognized as being bargained for by a collective bargaining agent, would have to formally satisfy himself that the employees involved were agreeable.

In other words, as the clause stands as originally drafted there is a certain obligation imposed upon the minister to decide whether or not the welfare of the employees has been safeguarded. My amendment would ensure, in my view, that the employees, whether or not they were organized into a collective bargaining unit, would have an opportunity of making their views known to the minister through some sort of official machinery prior to the minister being able unilaterally to decide. The employees would have a voice directly as to whether or not they considered that their welfare was being adequately taken care of, whereas under the original drafting of the clause it would be entirely at the discretion of a particular minister of labour. While I might go so far as to say that I have a certain amount of confidence that the present Minister of Labour would have due regard to the welfare of employees, that does not necessarily say that every minister of labour we might ever have in Canada would be, shall I say, as conscientious in looking into this matter as I would hope the present Minister of Labour would be. I believe that when we are considering legislation we have to have in mind not only the current situation, but future possible situations.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is the-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for York East.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could just-

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Who has the floor?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: -point out that what the hon. gentleman has said in his amendment is that if both groups do not agree, then the minister cannot use any discretion and in fact the application cannot be processed; and if both groups do agree, then the minister has to allow it. So we get back to an agreement between employer and employees without any discretion at all in the minister. I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would just define his amendment and see if it does not mean what I have said it means.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Not at all, Mr. Chairman, because I have not changed in any way the discretionary power of the minister as set forth in the original draft. It still says, "the minister, having regard to the conditions of employment in any industrial establishment and the welfare of the employees, may, by a permit in writing", and so on. I think this is a very important point, because the min-
Canada Labour Code
ister still has the overriding responsibility, as far as I am concerned, if this amendment I have proposed is accepted, of deciding whether or not there are particular circumstances that would justify the issuance of a permit; he still has the responsibility of deciding whether, even though a group of employees might apparently go along with the idea, their welfare would be adversely affected. Therefore my amendment, as I see it, does not in any way reduce the responsibility or authority of the minister as far as the operation of this clause is concerned; but it does ensure that there is an obligation on the minister to listen to the employees concerned, or their authorized representatives, just as under the original draft he would only act if, as and when, an employer takes the initiative. In other words, it provides for equal and co-initiative on the part of both the employer and the employee.
From such experience as I have had in situations where this practice prevailed, if there are reasonable grounds for an extension for overtime under certain conditions the employees are generally prepared, under normal relationships, to recognize that such is the situation. I may say that this arises in part out of some experience I have had in previous years as a responsible officer of a local union, where I was in the position of having to agree or disagree with a request from an employer for an overtime permit, and on the basis that the employees involved were prepared to go along with it, as the officer of that particular local union at that particular time I agreed that the arrangement could be made. If the normal and proper employer-employee relationship is in existence, and if there is justifiable reason under special circumstances for some extension of hours, then I think there is every likelihood that the employees would go along with a joint application. But if an employer is simply seeking to abuse his privileges and authority, then naturally there would be resistance from the employees.
I think the act should be so drafted that the minister will be made fully aware through some official requirement in the act of the views of the employees as a group, either informally or through their collective bargaining agent, before he could move on the granting of a permit. As I previously pointed out, this question does not affect the emergency provisions set out in clause 10, which enable overtime to be worked in the event of a breakdown or other emergency situation de-

Canada Labour Code
veloping, such as the tidal wave which occurred in the Alberni valley last year where the employer took the initiative to protect the plant and equipment and called out the employees without any question whatever. I feel this is the important principle which should be set out in the bill as far as any normal arrangement for special extension of hours is concerned.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the clause which the minister said might be used in the case of longshoremen. I intended to complain about the horrible bureaucratic mess I could visualize in applications for permits under this clause. I do not know how far the minister has taken his thoughts, but I am wondering whether in the case of the longshoremen in Halifax and Saint John one permit would do for the entire season, or whether there would be any difficulty with the various stevedores moving from ship to ship even in the course of one week.
In any event, I think that this amendment might bring the employees more into the picture; I do not think it is as earth shattering as the hon. member suggests. In fact, I cannot conceive of a situation where an application for a permit for these extra hours would go forward unless the employees and the employers both desired it. However, as I have said, the amendment looks all right to me because it does bring the employees more into the picture, which I think is desirable, at least in the case of the stevedores on the east coast.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having spent 15 years working as an employee and some 13 years as an employer, I have some difficulty with this amendment because I visualize the word "joint" as a possible roadblock whereby an application which is made will never reach the minister, in which case he would be unable to adjudicate on the question because a disagreement might have arisen in the meantime. This is the problem which I see.
Another problem here which I see is this. Where we have an administration, that administration is responsible for a particular plant or operation. Somebody has to call the shot; someone has to be in the harness; someone has to be in the driver's seat. If we were to get a situation where the management of a particular operation was no longer in the driver's seat, it would seem to me that we would be headed toward a deteriorating position. In the final analysis I think that any employer who remains an employer for very long is bound to have certain public relations

with his employees which could ascertain whether or not there was a willingness on the part of the majority of the employees to agree to go along with any application.
There are two different viewpoints in any operation; there is the viewpoint of management and the viewpoint of labour. Somewhere along the line these two viewpoints must, in order to establish a good operation, come together for the good of both employer and employee. I am a little troubled here by the word "joint" in the amendment which has been put forward in that it could serve as a roadblock to prevent the application ever getting to the minister's desk.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to support this amendment because I feel that to reach an agreement it is essential to consult the worker in order not to fall into a complete dictatorship.
One reads:
On the application of an employer or an employer's organization, the minister... may-
In my opinion, a very important factor, namely the worker, is being left out.
I feel that in the administration of this legislation the minister is acting only as a referee between the employer and the employee who will discuss a step which the legislation does not allow, and then ask the minister to prescribe an exemption from that legislation.
I feel that, as it stands now, the legislation leaves the door dangerously open as far as the employees' protection is concerned.
The present Minister of Labour is anxious to protect the employee but this legislation will be in force longer than one, two or three years.
For instance, if you had a minister who had very friendly relations with an employer, he could very well approve of labour conditions unfavorable to workers.
Therefore, I wish to inform you, Mr. Chairman, that for those reasons we shall support this amendment, and we shall do so in the workers' best interests.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I see some aspects of this amendment which are not at all desirable. I am pleased that there is provision for this extension to be granted and I have been assured that it could be used in cases similar to the stevedores in the shipping industry of this country, as mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert. However, if we were to follow the suggestion

of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I do not think the situation would be so good. I feel that he overlooks the fact that in Canada we are not dealing with an economy in which all or even nearly all of the employees have the benefit of the protection of collective bargaining or collective agreements. Many of the employees of this country and many of the employees to whom the act will apply are in the position that they do not have any unions to protect them.
Let me give an immediate example. Many of the employees of small radio stations in small towns in this country, other than the engineers-announcers and so forth-are not unionized and have no protection. I am sure there are many other examples in relation to federal jurisdiction.
This is bad legislation because it puts people who are not unionized and who do not have the protection of a trade union into the position where an employer can put pressure on them, for his own purposes, to join in his application for an extension of hours. I am sure the minister would not wish to be in the difficult position of turning down an application made jointly on behalf of an employer and his employees. However, in the case of these employees who are not unionized, and are without the protection of a union, employed in a business in the competitive market, they can be replaced very easily if they do not bend to the pressure placed on them to sign their employers' application for the extension of working hours. The employer in such a case could very easily suggest to those employees that unless they signed the application he would not be able to employ as many people on the staff. I think that is the main objection to the amendment.
Like the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I have observed many of these phoney objections placed before the labour relations board during certification hearings, in respect of which employees had been forced by their employers to sign them. I feel that exactly the same situation could occur in regard to this bill as a result of the amendment. The situation would be better as outlined by the bill without amendment, and for that reason I cannot support the amendment.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly to this amendment. Having listened with some interest to the arguments put forward by hon. members opposite I must state that I am still in opposition to the amendment. I appreciate the desire to protect workers. That is, of course, a general principle embodied in this bill.
Canada Labour Code
This particular clause authorizes, under certain circumstances, working hours in excess of 48 hours in respect of which the time and a half overtime provision prevails. Under clause 9 the minister is obliged to take into account the welfare of employees. A similar procedure is authorized under the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act which applies to the federal contracts. As the hon. member for Ontario appreciates, this type of application is often made by employers. In this case the worker is protected by the overtime provision and by the assurance that the minister of labour will take the employees' welfare into account.
It seems to me that we ought to take into account as well the employers' side of the situation. One of the functions of management is, of course, the scheduling of work hours. This is an important function which, in this case, is given to the employees or an employees' organization. It seems to me in this way we are entering excessively into something which is an accepted part of management function, namely the scheduling of hours of work.
Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied that the worker is fully protected under the provisions of this bill. It is also my desire to make sure that this bill does not become too restrictive, although I think it might if this additional veto power, as suggested by the amendment, is included. For that reason I must oppose the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Is the committee ready for the question?
Amendment (Mr. Barnett) negatived: Yeas, 52; nays, 79.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I declare the amendment lost.
Clause 9 agreed to.
On clause 10-Emergency work.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this clause seems to be vague. I presume it refers to the emergency operations of a business. While the marginal note refers to emergency work, nowhere else in the bill is emergency work mentioned or defined. I suggest there are many loopholes left which will lead to ultimate litigation. Perhaps the minister will explain what is meant in this clause by "serious interference"? How serious must the interference be?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
The purpose of clause 10, Mr. Chairman, is to provide an employer with an opportunity of scheduling hours be-

Canada Labour Code
yond the standard hours in order to meet emergency situations. However, wherever emergency work is required and the maximum weekly hours are exceeded, an employer must report in writing to the minister, within 15 days of the month end in which the maximum hours were exceeded, the number of employees who worked additional hours, the number of hours each employee worked, as well as the nature of the circumstances which necessitated the emergency work. This information must be reported to the minister, and in turn must be reported by the minister in his annual report to parliament. Hon. members must keep in mind the fact that any work schedule for emergency purposes beyond the maximum hours must be paid for at overtime rates. This clause provides some elbow room in the application of the provisions of the bill.
One thing we have attempted to do is to make the provisions of the bill as flexible as possible. This clause has relation to emergency work as a result of accidents to machinery, equipment, plants or persons, or to urgent and essential work to be done to machinery, equipment or plants, or other unforeseen or unpreventable circumstances, but only to the extent necessary to prevent serious interference with the ordinary working of the industrial establishment affected. This is a general clause, of course, but there is the overtime pay protection. Employers are not going to be anxious to incur additional expense unless the emergency is real.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the minister not agree that the expression "serious interference" is pretty loose and fairly broad? Who is going to determine whether or not the interference is serious?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: The employer, of course, will determine it himself, and remember that the employer normally will not be anxious to incur additional hours because of the additional expense. This is a deterrent against the exercise of this clause, except in emergency situations.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: I would still think this is fairly wide open. The union in the particular concern may not agree it is a serious interference. This certainly leaves the door wide open for litigation.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the Minister of Labour if the application of this clause is to include only maintenance or repair workers to repair machinery and equipment that may have broken down, or

would it extend as far as to include production workers who would be trying to catch up on lost production to meet quotas and deadlines that have arisen because of the machinery having broken down?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: No, the intent is not to provide a method of accelerating production activity. The intent is to provide additional hours to meet an emergency situation affecting machinery, equipment, plant or persons. I think the distinction appears in the clause. It is not intended to cover production activity.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: But the clause does not say that it shall be confined to maintenance or repair crews.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Paragraphs (a) and (b) imply, of course, that work of this kind is maintenance rather than production line work.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thought I heard the minister say in the course of his recent remarks when explaining the clause something to the effect that the reports that were filed with the minister would be part of the annual report of the Minister of Labour to parliament. I am not quite sure whether I heard the minister correctly. I do not see anything in the clause that makes any provision for that. First of all, would the minister tell me whether he did say what I thought I heard him say and, if so, what part of the clause requires that such a report be made to parliament?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: The clause itself makes no provision, but clause 49 obliges the Minister of Labour to include a statement in the annual report showing the additional hours worked by employees under permits issued by the minister under section 9 and the additional hours worked under section 10. Therefore this information will be contained in the report and will provide an opportunity for members in subsequent sessions to ascertain whether these sections are being abused in any way.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, section 10(2) reads partly as follows:
Where the maximum hours of work in an industrial establishment have been exceeded under the authority of this section-
Could the minister tell us whether the words "industrial establishment" cover only those establishments which come under the federal government or whether they apply to industrial establishments in general?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the expression "industrial establishment" is defined in subclause (g) of the interpretation clause.
"Industrial establishment" means any federal work, undertaking or business and includes such branch, section or other division of a federal work, undertaking or business as is designated as an industrial establishment by the regulations.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 11-Minimum hourly wage.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, clause 11 is the clause of the bill which sets out what is to be the minimum rate of wages under the general provisions of this legislation. I should like, as I believe I said on a previous occasion, to congratulate the minister on putting a figure in the bill and on making that figure one that applies right across Canada. I suspect it was not an easy battle for him to win. I suspect there were those involved in the drafting of the legislation who would have liked to leave it to regulation or to regional differentiations. So I say that I congratulate the minister on putting a figure in the bill and on making it national in its application.
However, the minister will not be surprised if I tell him once again that I think time has moved on and, indeed, has moved on even since the bill was first introduced, and that a figure of $1.25 an hour is not now high enough as a minimum wage. If one does a little arithmetic he will realize that $1.25 an hour for a 40 hour week works out to $50 a week. May I go further and suggest that if a person earns the minimum wage of $50 a week for 50 weeks in a year, allowing for two weeks annual vacation as set out in this legislation, that comes to a total of only $2,500 a year.
I remind the minister that it is now fairly generally accepted in the United States amongst social workers and government people as well that $3,000 a year is the poverty demarcation line. I suggest that the same figure is probably applicable to Canada. Surely if that is the case, surely if $3,000 a year merely indicates the line of demarcation between poverty and subsistence, it is hardly appropriate in 1965 for us to pass a minimum wage law that at best produces an annual income $500 below that figure.
Therefore I suggest that the figure should be changed to $1.50 an hour. If members will do the same kind of arithmetic I was doing a moment ago they will see that works out to $60 a week for a 40 hour week or $3,000
Canada Labour Code
a year for 50 weeks. If $3,000 a year is the line between poverty and subsistence, surely that is the least that we should be legislating in 1965. I see my hon. friend from Hamilton East glancing in my direction. In the last few weeks I had a good deal of opportunity to observe what was in his mind. I do not know for sure what is in it now, but he is probably thinking of the fact that there is still on the order paper a bill which I introduced on the first day of this session in which I suggested a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour. May I remind the hon. member for Hamilton East and the applauding member for Carleton that this session started one year ago today. Surely, a session that goes into its second year ought to move on a bit.
The fact that $1.25 is no longer a sufficient level for a minimum wage is also attested by the fact that the Canadian Labour Congress, which for years advocated $1.25 per hour, at its convention last April in Montreal amended this policy and proposed $1.50. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the action taken by the Canadian Labour Congress represents a reasonable stand and that the least we should do in parliament is to keep up with this kind of minimum.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, because I think that in 1965 we should be doing better than we were doing in 1964, because I think that when we are passing legislation of this kind we should make it as good as we can, I move:
That clause 11, subclause 1, be amended by deleting therefrom the words "one dollar and twenty five cents" and by substituting therefor the following words: "one dollar and fifty cents".
I submit, Mr. Chairman, this is a reasonable amendment, and that it is in keeping with the spirit of the legislation that the government has introduced after all these years. I would hope that the government would see fit to accept this amendment and thus make its own legislation a little better.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
In defence of this particular clause and in defence of the $1.25, I think it should be pointed out, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did point out, that he does have a bill on the order paper providing $1.25 as a minimum wage. It is true this was put on the order paper more than a year ago, in 1964. As he pointed out also, we have been in almost continuous session during that time and a lot of progressive legislation has gone through, much of which he has supported. I believe that when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre talks about $1.50, no one could argue that

Canada Labour Code
$1.50 could be considered an adequate wage. Even if it worked out to $60 per week or $3,000 per year, I think it could be established that it would not be adequate for a man with a family. It certainly is a subsistence or below subsistence level. All of these arguments can be advanced, but I am not so sure they are pertinent to this particular bill.
One thing the hon. member did not emphasize in his remarks is the fact that this is minimal legislation. We are not advocating across the country that this is what should be paid or even acknowledging that it is an acceptable standard. This is minimal legislation, and is the point below which wages should not fall. This is the aspect that should be emphasized as the governing factor in the minds of members when they vote for this legislation. As the hon. member knows, we are well ahead of many provincial legislatures in this field and if we were to set a higher standard it would not be realistic. As the hon. member pointed out when we were dealing with the clause concerning hours, this legislation is ahead of legislation passed by the provincial legislatures, which covers ever so many more employees than fall under federal jurisdiction. We are hoping that by the passage of this measure we will be applying a pressure point to provincial legislatures to pass similar legislation making this a minimum standard. I am not so sure, when you are dealing with minimal standards, that you are unrealistic not to realize that you will defeat the very purpose of your legislation by discouraging many provincial legislatures from any real attempt at improving their legislation. We want to achieve that degree of uniformity that will benefit ever so many more employees who would be affected by such provincial legislation.
The hon. member talked about the United States, Mr. Chairman; their congress has been dealing with this minimum wage legislation for some time. In certain areas, no doubt they are now up to $1.25. The late President Kennedy had great difficulty in pushing $1.15 through congress. Even today a substantial segment of the labour force has been exempted from the legislation. Many of the people who would benefit most from such legislation have been exempted from its provisions. So far as the Canadian federal authority is concerned, I believe we are well ahead of the United States. We have resisted this very tendency that has been so prevalent
IMr. Munro.]
in the United States; the tendency to make exemptions.
Then, too, it has been advocated by many of those authorities in the United States and Canada who have studied poverty that $1.25 should be the minimum wage. They are not saying that minimum wage legislation is the all important type of legislation so far as combatting poverty is concerned. What they are in fact saying is that it is a factor and only a factor. They emphasize the fact that it should be considered minimal. I do not know if the official New Democratic party platform has been changed, Mr. Chairman, but the last formal policy announcement I saw advocated $1.25. I am aware that the last formal representations made to the government by the Canadian Labour Congress, I believe in December, 1963, a little over a year ago, advocated $1.25 as the minimum wage.
I believe the government can say, in view of the study and preparation that has gone into this bill, in view of the representations favouring $1.25, in view of the studies on poverty and in view of the fact we are advocating this as a minimal standard only, that to go any higher at this time when so many other provincial governments are not anywhere near this level, is being unrealistic.

Clause 11 and the amendment made to it raise what is, in my judgment, possibly the most important element in relation to this labour standard. I should like to begin by saying that this standard of

Canada Labour Code
$1.25 an hour is the most advanced and progressive and far reaching standard established on this continent. The United States government under the regime of the late President Kennedy was regarded as having taken one of the most important steps in the labour field by establishing a minimum wage of $1.25. But this was a rate to be reached only progressively. Moreover, that legislation does not initially cover a large proportion of the employees. In this bill, despite the fact that general wage levels in the United States are considerably higher than those in Canada, we are establishing a rate of $1.25 across the country on July 1, no differentiation being made between one part of Canada and another. It is the best standard which has ever been introduced on this continent-much better than in the United States where a start was made at $1.

speechtext: So was $2 wheat. So was medicare. So was the Canada pension plan in a form which called for higher figures than we have today. The minister did not try to trade on Liberal party platforms in the last elections; he contended that the Canadian Labour Congress changed its policy after it had learned of the policy of the government, and I have put the record straight. The policy of the government was made clear in this bill on October 1, 1964. The hon. member for Hamilton West may laugh, but surely he can read, and the fact is that the Canadian Labour Congress asked for $1.50 last spring.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the hon. member indicating that he himself, for instance, received no indication prior to October 1, 1964, that it was the intention of this administration to bring in the figure of $1.25?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: There were many rumours that the government did intend to bring it in and many statements were made. Surely hon. members opposite have been around here long enough to know that you must wait for government policy until it is announced by the government. I am suggesting that the Minister of Labour made a misstatement when he said the Canadian Labour Congress changed its policy after the government's policy had been announced.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I did not say that at all.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: We will let the record speak for itself, but let it be clear that the Canadian Labour Congress changed its policy in this matter in April of 1964.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Could I ask the hon. member whether there was any communication between some of the members here who heard it could be $1.25 and the Canadian Labour Congress?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would tell the hon. member and other hon. members opposite that during the two years between the 1962 and 1964 conventions of the Canadian Labour Congress many sections of that movement were sending in resolutions asking the congress to change its policy. Quite frankly, I do not think we need spend much time on this, but the point I am making is that hon. members opposite certainly have not much to argue about or have not much substance if they are trying to trade on the fact that the Canadian Labour Congress and the member for Winnipeg North Centre prior to last April suggested $1.25. Ten years ago I suggested $1. In light of the economic needs of the people today I would suggest that $1.25 an hour, or $50 a week, or $2,500 a year is not enough. The figure should now be $1.50.
I can also tell the Minister of Labour and the hon. member for Hamilton East, as they both know, that the Canadian Labour Congress is appearing before the government again on March 10. Many of us who have been invited to the reception which will be held afterwards know officially of that date, and
Canada Labour Code
I am sure that everybody in this chamber can readily guess that in the brief that the Canadian Labour Congress will present on that occasion when it speaks on minimum wages it will base its request on what the last convention of the Canadian Labour Congress asked for. What the last convention asked for was $1.50, and I suggest that hon. members opposite are just running for cover if they are trying to find support for their position in the position taken by the Canadian Labour Congress and others in times gone by.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member one question. Is he sure that the policy statement was issued at the annual convention of the congress, or was it issued in connection with a meeting of the executive council?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Among the resolutions moved at the convention of the Canadian Labour Congress-the Minister of Labour was there on one occasion, and being there myself I heard him speak on this same subject although he did not name a figure-were several asking for the policy to be changed so as to make the figure $1.50 an hour. Those resolutions were not reached at the convention itself-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Hon. members say "Oh, oh", but the executive council confirmed the change soon after the convention and I would suggest to these members who are so gleeful about this, especially the members from industrial areas, that they go back to those industrial areas and attend the meetings of labour councils in those areas and reflect the kind of attitude they are showing tonight and see what happens.

speechtext:
Since the hon. member has suggested that we go back to our constituencies and see what the workers in those areas are saying in connection with what the figure should be, is the hon. member aware that less than two months ago the Nova Scotia federation of labour, an affiliate of the Canadian Labour Congress, made a presentation to the provincial government to the effect

Canada Labour Code
that the minimum wage should be set at a figure considerably below the figure the hon. member is suggesting in his amendment?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Knowing some of the economic conditions of the maritime provinces I can well imagine that requests of that sort might be made for a minimum less than this, as a minimum for a particular area or a particular province.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting then that there should be area rates in Canada?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, not at all. As a matter of fact, one of the reasons I want the minimum wage rate in national legislation to be an adequate rate is because I want it to result in pressure being put on the provinces to bring their rates up. I think it is a disgrace that across Canada there are rates as low as the Minister of Labour was able to quote tonight, and he did not quote the lowest ones. If he were to give the figures for right across the country the picture would be shameful. If he gave us the figures with respect to the provinces where the Liberals are in power, especially in relation to Newfoundland, we would then see the disgraceful picture which exists. Surely after all the talk the Liberals have indulged in about the lead they are going to give during these exciting days of decision, we should come to the conclusion that the thing to do today is come forward with something that is really progressive and adequate, considering present conditions.
The hon. member for Hamilton East suggested that this legislation deals only in minimal standards and is not legislation which seeks to set going or standard rates which are adequate. I think his suggestion was that this legislation sets a figure below which no wage should fall. The issue is put squarely before the member for Hamilton East and his colleagues. Where do they want to set that figure below which wages should not fall? I accept his definition and agree that we are not setting fair wages or wages which will provide a modest living, or wages which will meet the needs of people, but that rather we are setting a figure below which wages should not fall. Is he suggesting that the Liberal party is supporting a minimum wage in the year 1965 of $3,000 a year or $2,500 a year? If he votes against this amendment he is in effect saying that $2,500 a year is the figure below which wages

should not fall but that they can fall below $3,000.
Mr. Chairman, I give again my full commendation to the Minister of Labour for the battle I know he must have put up in the cabinet in order to persuade the government to proceed with this bill. I believe that it is an advantage to have a figure set, but why not go first class; why not do the job adequately if it is to be done at all?
Some of my conversation tonight across the floor has been with the Minister of Labour and the hon. member for Hamilton East. I have been interested in both those gentlemen since they came into this house, and I have been impressed by the suggestion which has been made that they are examples of the new young Liberals-the people who are going to rejuvenate the party and give us a new forward-looking approach.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Order, please. May I suggest to the hon. member who now has the floor that he is perhaps going beyond the scope of the clause now before us for consideration.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say something in respect of what those two gentlemen in particular have said about my amendment to increase the minimum hourly wage from $1.25 to $1.50.
What they have said about this amendment is that it defeats the very purpose I have in mind. As I suggested, Mr. Chairman, it was my understanding that these were examples of the new young Liberals, but they speak in the same way the Secretary of State for External Affairs used to speak to me in this house and in the corridors, when he was minister of national health and welfare ten or 20 years ago. In those days that hon. gentleman said to me: Stanley, what you are doing is defeating the very purpose you have in mind, in reference to increases to old age pensions or the establishment of medicare.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, when he speaks about what happened ten, 20 or 30 years ago, that some of us are not so preoccupied with what took place in the past, but concerned with what is happening at the present and what will happen in the future. At the present time here in Ontario, having regard to this federal legislation, which is certainly progressive,

there has been a commission studying the effects of minimum wages on a greater number of employees in the construction industry than all the employees affected by this legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Order, please. I should like to remind the hon. member for Hamilton East that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has the floor. Perhaps the hon. member for Hamilton East will make a speech when that hon. member has concluded.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be allowed to answer the question put to me by the hon. member for Hamilton East. He has suggested that some of us should not be so concerned with what happened in the past, and that he and some of his colleagues are concerned with the future. The point I am trying to make is that he has put himself back into the past by taking the same approach as did his forebears in the Liberal party, suggesting that my amendment defeats the purpose I have in mind. I know very well that if the hon. member for Hamilton East and the Minister of Labour were sitting on this side of the house at a time when this kind of legislation was before us for discussion they would be pushing for these benefits and asking that the minimum standards be increased. I am asking them to take the same attitude toward social progress and toward this legislation at this time, when they have the responsibility of government and are in a position to do something about this, that they would take if they were on this side of the house, and which they did take at the time they were here.
At this time, in the mid 1960's, $3,000 per year has been recognized in North America as a salary which is at the breaking point between poverty and existence. Surely any minimum wage to be set by this parliament should be set at least at that figure.
Again I congratulate the minister for bringing this bill before parliament, because some of it is good; but at the same time I must ask him why he does not make it better. That is exactly what we are trying to allow him to do in proposing this amendment to increase the hourly rate from $1.25 to $1.50.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think there is one fundamental difference between legislating for minimum wages and legislating wages. It seems to me that the amendment the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has put forward, because of his own argument, goes beyond the national minimum wage which should be set at this time. The
Canada Labour Code
hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre cited the minimum wage rate covered by provincial legislation. Obviously the rate set by this bill must apply not only to the most highly industrialized parts of Canada but all across Canada and, therefore, must be realistic.
The whole crux of the hon. member's argument hangs on his own personal embarrassment at having introduced a bill setting the basic rate at $1.25 per hour. He now says he would like to move forward one year, although he does not offer any particular standard to be followed in moving forward that year. He merely suggests that we increase the minimum hourly rate by 25 cents, or roughly 20 per cent. That is a very good increase for a one-year period, and one which could not be sustained on any cumulative basis. If the hon. member was concerned about offering some regular yardstick by which we could advance the minimum wage rates under a defensible plan, or a plan bearing some relationship to reality, he might have argued that it should be related to the cost of living, or some other reasonable indicator. However, the hon. member does not offer any yardstick at all, but merely picks the $1.50 figure out of the air. As the Minister of Labour has pointed out, if the $1.50 figure had been set by this bill, I am sure the hon. member would have suggested $1.75.
The hon. member does not argue in terms of regular standards in respect of which a minimum wage rate could be established, such as the cost of living or some indicator related to the productivity, but, rather, suggests a figure which is not in reality a minimum wage. He is moving beyond the purposes of minimum wage rate legislation into a field which, as far as I am concerned, should be occupied only by union-management bargaining processes. This is a field in which I hope there will be more productive advances made by those bargaining processes than could ever be made by legislation in respect of something of this nature.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago we heard a bragging contest between the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). According to them, Canadian workers have had some relief only since this government took office.
We heard the Minister of Labour state the minimum salaries in various provinces,

Canada Labour Code
but we also noticed that he failed to mention the provinces which are under a Liberal administration.
Since I am from the province of Quebec, I would have liked the Minister of Labour to indicate the minimum salary in that province. I would also have liked him to tell us what is the minimum salary in New Brunswick and Newfoundland. But it so happens that those three provinces are under Liberal governments, and it is a well known fact that under a Liberal provincial administration the average salary of workers is lower than in the other provinces. That is why the minister failed to give us that information.
But there is more than that as far as this bill is concerned. Being from the province of Quebec I do not hesitate to say that this Bill No. C-126 is a discriminatory measure for the province of Quebec. For instance, if we read clause 11 of this bill, we see that:
(1) Except as otherwise provided by or under this Part, an employer shall pay to each employee of the age of 17 years and over-
It so happens that in the province of Quebec one may work as soon as one reaches the age of 14. You realize therefore that, between the ages of 14 and 17, there is discrimination against workers employed in federal establishments.
The minister can take all the credit he wants for the welfare and comfort of the working class, he will never convince us that the measure he is proposing now is not a discrimination against the people of Quebec.
Having been for many years in a position to provide jobs for my fellow citizens, I can say that I hired dozens of workers from 14 to 17 years old who were the breadwinners of entire families, orphans and needy mothers. Consequently, the proposal under consideration is a striking example of what the present administration has in mind. It is nothing but window dressing and the government did not intend to help the people when they introduced that piece of legislation.
I urge them to stop bragging about themselves and to get down to the level of the small wage earners by introducing legislation which would be more helpful for the people in general.
I am not surprised to hear that New Democrats are calling for a minimum of $1.50 an hour. On that point I share the opinion of my friend the Minister of Labour. If he had suggested a minimum of $1.50, they would have called for $1.75 or $2.00. Well, they

know they will never have to keep their promises, and that is why they so readily promise $1.50, $1.75 or $2.00.
Personally, I ask the Minister of Labour to amend his bill so that it will not be discriminatory to the citizens of Quebec.
I make this suggestion most humbly and in all objectivity, so that people will stop suggesting we are spending our time enacting laws or passing legislation discriminatory to the province of Quebec. There could be no better opportunity for the Minister of Labour to refute this argument put forward by the extremists in my province.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question?

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Two, if you wish.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Does he know that as a member of parliament he can move an amendment? If he is not happy with the wording of clause 11, he can move an amendment and the house will vote on it. The hon. member does not have to beg or implore the Minister of Labour; as a member of the house, he can move an amendment to the bill.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in reply to my hon. friend from Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes, I must say that I did not move an amendment because I wanted to give the Liberal government the opportunity to improve its political fortune which is at a low point. I am helping the government out of charity.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before we conclude the debate this evening I should like to make the following remarks. First of all, may I say there are certainly many aspects of this legislation that appeal to me and I am sure to many of the people in my riding. I am forced to speak at this time, however, because the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has brought up something that I think every member of the house should be concerned about at the present time.
The other day I read certain statistics compiled by the Ontario federation of labour which showed that a family of four living on a total annual income of under $2,000 a year was living in absolute destitution, that a family of four with a total annual income of only $3,000 per annum was living in grinding poverty and that a family of four with a total annual income of under $4,000 a year, having in mind the standard of living in the nation at large, was living in a state of deprivation. I think every member of the house

must realize that here in a country where we have the second highest economic standard of living in the world we have done a terribly poor job of pushing back the frontiers of poverty and want. It is all very well to talk about poverty in the countries of Africa and Asia, but here in Canada 35 per cent of our population are living in a state of deprivation, destitution or poverty.
I do not say this in a political sense at all. I say it simply to bring forward the point I wish to make, and I do not think that anybody with a conscience can quibble with the statistics of the Ontario federation of labour. Any family of four with a total income under $4,000 is certainly living in deprivation, with a total income under $3,000 in poverty and under $2,000 in destitution.
I realize and recognize the fine aspects of the bill as do most members of the house, but let us not for a moment overestimate the effects. We are in fact setting a minimum standard which is within the area of poverty for a family of four with a total income of under $3,000 per year. I hope we recognize this as we are doing it.
The minister recognizes that a family of four, no matter where they are living in Canada, in Newfoundland or Quebec or any of the other provinces, cannot live on a total income of $3,000 unless they are living in poverty. I will say this categorically. Every member recognizes this. We know that in passing this legislation here in Canada we will have done a poor job in pushing back the frontiers of poverty.
I am ready to support this legislation, but I feel also that the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should be listened to with great care tonight.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Question, question.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I hear some members
calling "Question". I know that one of them will be the hon. member for Hamilton West, and one will be the hon. member for Jacques Cartier-Lasalle. They never get up to say anything themselves. I should like to answer the minister. I do not know how the members of my party will vote on this issue, but I know how I feel. However, nobody on this side of the house is criticizing the minister for introducing this kind of legislation. Nobody is criticizing the minister for introducing minimum wage legislation.
However, I say to you that if you are going to legislate to put a floor under wages, and if it is to be of any use to humanity, let us 20220-728
Canada Labour Code
do something worth while. You are really not declaring war on poverty, you are freezing these people in poverty. Hon. members know as well as I do that if we legislate a wage rate of $1.25 there will be a lot of employers in this country who will use it as an excuse and say that is the amount of money these people are going to get. In other words, we are freezing wages. We are freezing these people in poverty. We are not declaring war on poverty.
It is no answer, Mr. Chairman, to say we are doing better than the United States. Is this what this government is going to do? Is this a government that is going to say we are going to implement everything the United States does? Is this your program? I say to you, and to the minister, that is not good enough. I say if we are going to do a job tonight we should take a hard, logical look at the situation. If we are going to have a minimum wage, then let us establish it at $1.50. Let us not freeze it at $1.25. Let us have some flexibility in the bill, Mr. Chairman.
Certain powers have been assigned to the minister. This may be an area in which powers should be assigned to the minister so that the legislation can be made more flexible. Within the last few months, in fact within the last year, the cost of living has increased. When the cost of living is increasing, what is the use in chaining workers to a minimum wage which does not fit that cost of living? I want to be fair to the government. The cost of living has been escalating for some time. In fact, there has been a gradual escalation in the cost of living ever since the last war. Let us face it. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that just because he proposed a bill establishing $1.25 as a minimum wage is no reason for establishing that rate today. We should have some flexibility today. If we are going to declare war on poverty, let us do a job.
I know that you have had a hard time getting this measure through cabinet. I believe any minister of labour would have had a hard time selling this measure to any cabinet. The fact is, however, it is not doing the job we want it to do. Perhaps I was a little unkind in some of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, when I said there were politics behind this bill. If you really want to be politicians, then let us set a minimum wage which is reasonable, one upon which the average man can live. Then, I will say you are doing a job in that regard. The argument which has been advanced that the province

Canada Labour Code
of Ontario, Alberta or Saskatchewan has a minimum wage of a certain amount does not answer anything. I suggest to the minister sincerely that I have read the bill. I know its terms, and I know you can enlarge them. However, basically, you are not only setting a minimum wage, you are freezing the hours of work. Many of these pieces of legislation in the provinces allow overtime, and it is by the use of the overtime provision that workers are able to make a living. Instead of limiting these workers to 40 hours per week, what you are doing is imposing on them the necessity of working another 40 hours in order to make a living. In other words, you are really legislating an 80 hour week; let us face it.

-instead of 17 years, so that there be no discrimination against workers in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Is it only in the province of Quebec that 14 year old children work, or is it the same in all provinces? It must be noted that the preamble reads as follows:
An act respecting hours of work in federal undertakings and businesses.
-and not in all undertakings.

maintopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my argument is even more sound since a specific age is mentioned. This means that the present minister has considered all those things and has decided that even in the province of Quebec, where some people have to work as early as 14 years old, the latter are not included and will not be able to earn $1.25 per hour before being 17 years old.
This is what I want to draw to the attention of the house and it is to correct this anomaly that I ask my hon. colleagues from

the province of Quebec to help me do away with this discrimination in regard to Quebec workers.
I am sorry if they do not realize the significance of this measure, but as far as I am concerned, I wish to call the attention of the house to the importance for the workers of the province of Quebec to be treated in the same way as those of other Canadian provinces.

speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall continue our consideration of the labour standards legislation, and when that is completed I would hope we can deal with some other matters on the order paper. Perhaps it would be useful if I were to indicate some of them, not necessarily in order of priority, so that
Business of the House
they may be on the record where members can refer to them.
There is the resolution and legislation on the Coal Production Assistance Act, item 58 on the order paper; the insurance and trust company legislation amendments, item 76; the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act amendment, item 54; and the Companies Act amendments, item 92. I would ask hon. members to look at this legislation with a view to the possibility of referring it to the banking and commerce committee for immediate study and return to the house.
Then there is the act respecting the Geneva conventions, item 48 on the order paper; the act amending the Privileges and Immunities (United Nations) Act, item 52; the Senate retirement legislation, item 40; the amendments to the international tax agreements, a bill which was given first reading today; the amendment to the Penitentiary Act, another bill which was given first reading today; the Canada Shipping Act, which I understand is now in committee, and the second reading of Bill No. S-2, respecting the Revised Statutes of Canada, item No. 15 on the order paper. I would call tomorrow any one of those items that would be agreeable to the house leaders of the opposition groups, after we have finished the labour standards bill.
It being seven minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
